metaDescription: Five Midea dehumidifiers from 20 to 50 pints compared by noise rating, pump and filter design, so you can match a traditional cabinet to a bedroom or basement.
expertTake: The Midea 50-pint with the built-in pump is the pick for a large basement where noise matters, since it pairs a quiet-operation claim with a pump that moves water to a distant drain. The 35-pint with the reusable filter is the value pick for a mid-size room. If you want the squat Cube cabinet with an oversized tank, look at the separate Cube guide instead.
introParagraphs: Mainstream compressor dehumidifiers share a family resemblance: a tall cabinet, a front bucket, a washable filter and a humidistat. What sets one maker's line apart is how quiet it is on low, how it handles drainage and how well the filter and controls hold up in daily use.

The practical route is to pick the capacity step for the room, then compare noise, pump and filter details. Those smaller features decide whether the machine fades into the background or becomes something you resent.

products.name: Midea 50-Pint Dehumidifier with Built-In Pump, 4,500 Sq Ft

specList.label: Pump
specList.value: Built in, drains vertically or horizontally

products.description:
The pumped 50-pint is the Midea to pick when the basement has no floor drain within reach. A built-in pump moves water away from the machine, so the discharge hose can climb to a utility sink or run across the room to a drain. Many tall-cabinet units of this size rely on gravity alone, which is the reason the pump variant matters.

The listing rates it for up to 4,500 square feet and calls the operation ultra quiet, which suits a basement that doubles as a living area. Against the 35-pint it adds fifteen pints, and against the plain 50-pint it adds drain flexibility at a higher cost. Energy Star certification helps keep a summer of running time affordable.

In ownership, the pump is the part to respect. Test it when the humid season begins, keep the hose from kinking behind the cabinet and rinse the filter on a schedule. If a floor drain sits next to the machine, the plain 50-pint gives the same drying power with one component less to look after.
products.bestFor: Large basements without a floor drain nearby.
pros: Built-in pump drains up or across a room
Ultra quiet operation claim suits finished spaces
Energy Star certified with 4,500 square foot rating
Fifteen more pints than the 35-pint model

products.name: Midea 50-Pint Wi-Fi Dehumidifier for Basement, 4,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
This is the same 50-pint class with app control instead of a pump. It states a noise level of 49 dBA in low mode, which is a measured-on-the-bench style figure that tells you how it sounds when it is only maintaining a room, not pulling it down from a wet spell. Wi-Fi lets you set the target and read status from a phone.

Compared with the pumped version, the drain is the difference: this unit uses a gravity hose or its bucket. That is fine in a basement with a floor drain. It is a poor fit where the drain is uphill, so measure before you order.

In ownership, the app is the convenience and the filter is the chore. Confirm the panel still holds a setpoint when the router is off, wash the filter every few weeks and place a separate hygrometer in the farthest corner. For a rental or a seasonal house, the remote view of humidity is the real benefit.
products.bestFor: Large basements with a floor drain and a need for remote monitoring.
pros: Wi-Fi smart control for remote changes
Stated 49 dBA on low mode
50-pint capacity rated to 4,500 square feet
Energy Star certified
cons: No pump, so the drain must run downhill
Noise figure applies to low mode only

products.name: Midea 35-Pint Dehumidifier with Reusable Air Filter, 3,000 Sq Ft
products.description:
The 35-pint is the middle rung of the traditional Midea ladder and the one that fits the widest range of homes. It carries a reusable air filter, a stated 49 dBA on low mode and a 3,000 square foot rating. That puts it in the sweet spot for a mid-size basement or a large bedroom.

Fifteen pints separate it from the 50-pint models, and thirteen separate it from the 22-pint. In a space with a steady but moderate problem it cycles off between wet spells, which is kind to the compressor and the electric bill. In a wet unfinished basement, step up.

The reusable filter is the ownership detail that saves money: you wash it rather than buy replacements. Keep a second filter if the model allows, so one can dry while the other works. Empty the bucket or use a hose, and keep the cabinet a hand-width from the wall.
products.bestFor: Mid-size basements and large bedrooms with moderate dampness.
pros: Reusable air filter avoids replacement cost
Stated 49 dBA on low mode
35-pint capacity for rooms up to 3,000 square feet
Balanced size for most homes
cons: Underpowered for a wet unfinished basement
No pump option at this size

products.name: Midea 22-Pint Energy Star Dehumidifier for Basement, 1,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
The 22-pint is the smallest of the tall-cabinet Mideas and the quietest on paper, with a stated 47 dBA. Rated coverage tops out at 1,500 square feet and Energy Star certification is listed, which suits a bedroom or small-room machine.

On the current federal test of 65F and 60% RH, 22 pints is stronger than it sounds, since the older label scale would have called it about 30 pints. Even so, it has a smaller coil and bucket than the 35-pint, so it belongs in a closed room, not an open basement.

It is light enough to move between rooms, and the low noise suits sleeping spaces. Use a hose or empty the bucket daily in a damp room, rinse the filter monthly and keep the door closed so the machine only treats a small volume of air.
products.bestFor: Bedrooms, bathrooms and small closed rooms.
pros: Stated 47 dBA, the lowest in this lineup
Energy Star certified

products.name: Midea Cube 20-Pint Dehumidifier, 1,500 Sq Ft with Drain Hose
products.description:
The only squat cube in this guide, the 20-pint is here for owners who want a small footprint and an oversized tank. The listing advertises a tank up to three times larger than the older design and a drain hose for continuous running, with 1,500 square feet of coverage.

Against the 22-pint tall unit it gives up two pints and a quieter spec, but it fits into a tight corner and runs on a hose more easily. If a low cabinet suits your space better than a tall one, this is the compromise. For larger spaces, the dedicated Cube guide covers the 35-pint and 50-pint versions.

Upkeep is the same as the rest: rinse the filter, keep the hose clear and give the intake room. It is a closed-room machine, so do not ask it to dry an open basement.
products.bestFor: Small rooms where a low, compact cabinet fits best.
pros: Compact cube cabinet fits tight corners
Tank advertised as up to three times larger
Drain hose supports continuous running
Energy Star certified
cons: Only 1,500 square feet of listed coverage

buyingCriteria.explanation: The traditional Midea cabinets here come in 22, 35 and 50 pint steps, rated for roughly 1,500, 3,000 and 4,500 square feet. A bedroom suits the 22-pint, a mid-size basement the 35-pint and a large or damp basement a 50-pint. When the room smells musty, go up a step so the machine cycles off rather than grinding on. Remember that the coverage label assumes open floor, so closed doors in a divided basement split it into separate small spaces and one cabinet in a single room leaves the rest damp.

The 22-pint lists 47 dBA, while the 35-pint and the Wi-Fi 50-pint list 49 dBA on low mode. A decibel figure at low speed tells you how it sounds while maintaining a room, not while pulling down a wet space. Expect more noise at full speed, and place the machine away from sleeping areas. A compressor also cycles on and off, so the click and the change in pitch at start-up are often more noticeable at night than the steady hum.

The pumped 50-pint lifts water vertically or sends it across the room, while the plain 50-pint, the 35-pint and the 22-pint rely on gravity. Measure the climb from the machine to the discharge before choosing. A pump costs more but fixes a layout that a gravity hose cannot. Check the hose length as well, because a long flat run reduces the effective lift and a sagging loop can hold water and slow the flow.

The 35-pint advertises a reusable air filter, which you wash instead of replacing. A washable filter saves money, but only if you actually wash it every few weeks. A clogged filter quietly cuts airflow and invites frost on the coil. Keep a calendar reminder rather than trusting memory, and dry the filter completely before refitting it so it does not grow a film.

Only the Wi-Fi 50-pint lists app control in this guide. It helps for second homes and rentals where you cannot see the machine. Check that the panel works as a fallback if the network drops. Remote status is genuinely useful for a vacation house, where a full bucket or a tripped breaker can sit unnoticed for a week while humidity climbs.

A tall cabinet has a larger air path per square foot of floor, while the Cube 20-pint trades that for a low profile and a bigger tank. Choose by where it will sit: a corner with headroom suits tall, and a spot under a shelf suits a cube. Whichever shape you choose, leave a hand-width of clearance at the intake and exhaust, since a blocked grille is the most common reason a good machine looks weak.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity ladder
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 22, 35 and 50 pint steps and their listed coverage of 1,500, 3,000 and 4,500 square feet. With three distinct steps, matching capacity to the room takes little guesswork. We treated ratings as spec sheet figures, not measurements.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the stated sound levels, 47 dBA on the 22-pint and 49 dBA on the 35-pint and Wi-Fi 50-pint. We treated them as low-mode figures. Quieter spec sheets scored better for bedrooms. We also discounted any noise claim that did not name a fan setting, because a figure without a speed attached tells you little about real use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drain flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the pump on one 50-pint with the gravity hose on the others. The pump scored highest for awkward layouts. Simple hose ports scored well for simplicity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Filter and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the reusable filter on the 35-pint and the general washable approach across the range. Cheap upkeep helps in year-three ownership. A filter that is easy to remove scores higher, since a hard-to-reach filter is the one that gets skipped. We also considered how easily the bucket slides out and whether the handle feels sturdy when the bucket is full.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across the range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared relative price tiers from the 20 and 22 pint units at the low end to the pump model at the top. The best value is the smallest unit that handles the room.

cards.label: Pump (50-Pint with Pump)
cards.text: Lifts water up or across a room, so it works when a floor drain is not nearby. It adds a part and a cost. It suits large basements with awkward plumbing.

cards.label: Gravity (50-Pint Wi-Fi, 35-Pint, 22-Pint, Cube 20)
cards.text: Simpler and cheaper, with nothing extra to fail. It needs a downhill hose or manual emptying. It suits spaces with a floor drain.

howToChoose.note: Choose the pump when the drain is uphill or far, and gravity when a floor drain is close.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A low stated noise level, a cabinet that fits beside a bed and a capacity that does not run constantly. Closed doors help the machine do its job.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 22-Pint is the quietest on paper, the 35-Pint suits a large bedroom and the Cube 20-Pint fits a tight corner.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The drain is uphill, the space is large or you want remote status. The pumped 50-Pint and the Wi-Fi 50-Pint earn their cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The room is a bedroom or small basement. The 22-Pint, 35-Pint or Cube 20-Pint cover it for less.

maintenance.why: A clogged filter chokes airflow and lets frost form on the coil. Rinse it, dry it fully and refit it dry.
Stale water grows a film that smells. A rinse with mild soap and a thorough dry stops it from returning.
A pump idle all winter can stick. Run a cycle and watch the discharge until the flow is steady.
Kinks and sediment cause overflow. Pour a cup of water through to confirm the flow.
Lint on the coil reduces heat transfer and is the usual reason for slow drying in the third summer. Unplug before opening.

faq.q: Which Midea size do I need?
faq.a: A bedroom suits the 22-pint, a mid-size basement suits the 35-pint and a large or damp basement suits a 50-pint. If the room smells musty or shows condensation, go up a step so the machine cycles off between wet spells.
The 22-pint states 47 dBA and the 35-pint and Wi-Fi 50-pint state 49 dBA on low mode. Those are low-speed figures, so expect more sound while the machine is pulling down a wet room.

faq.q: Is the pump model worth it?
faq.a: Yes when the drain is above the machine or far from it. With a floor drain nearby, the plain Wi-Fi 50-pint does the same drying without a pump to maintain.

faq.q: How does this differ from the Cube models?
faq.a: The Cube line is a squat cabinet with an oversized tank, while this range uses a traditional tall cabinet and a front bucket. The Cube 20-pint appears here as a compact option for small rooms.
Compressor dehumidifiers commonly last 5 to 10 years. Cleaning the filter and coil and choosing the right size are the main levers.

A target of 40 to 50 percent suits most rooms. Damp air above 60 percent invites mold, and below 30 percent the room feels parched. A built-in sensor can be a few points off, so a cheap meter placed away from the Midea tells you whether the whole room is dry or only the air beside it.
